other_side: Zitron would say OpenClaw 2.0 is the problem dressed up as the solution. In his manifesto he describes every AI power-user's setup as a contrived chain of harnesses, prompts and API calls that needs constant maintenance to do some things some of the time — and he cites an OpenClaw agent deleting a security researcher's emails as the kind of thing that happens when you hand a 'mindless software tool' the keys to your files. Four years and a trillion-plus dollars in, he argues, the best on offer is software that 'kind of worked' after repeated bonking, sold as autonomous while blaming the user for its failures. Adding a second person to the session, on his view, doesn't make the agent trustworthy; it just spreads the babysitting across a team, and none of it survives the moment enterprises notice the token bill and cut the budget.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is reliability at the point of use — whether an agent works well enough, often enough, that a person keeps it. Both accept as fact that today's harnesses are fragile: NLW's own show quotes a power user saying updates break his setup most of the time; Zitron's manifesto describes the same experience with more contempt. The empirical question that will resolve is retention — do people who set up OpenClaw or Hermes still use them daily six months on, or hop and lapse? The observable is credible usage data for these tools and whether enterprise token budgets rise or fall. The worldview residue is whether fragility is early-stage noise or intrinsic. NLW is vindicated if breakage falls release by release and shared sessions reach mainstream products; Zitron if the tinkerers plateau and budgets shrink. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is that both agree the tools are too brittle for ordinary users today. Watch whether a big lab copies the multiplayer pattern.
